content: Lipids are a diverse group of naturally occurring molecules that are soluble in nonpolar solvents but insoluble in water. They include fats, oils, waxes, cholesterol, sterols, fat-soluble vitamins (A, D, E, and K), monoglycerides, diglycerides, phospholipids, and other related compounds. Lipids serve several critical biological functions, including energy storage, forming structural components of cell membranes, and acting as signaling molecules. While the term lipid is sometimes used interchangeably with fat, fats are specifically a subgroup of lipids known as triglycerides, which should not be confused with fatty acids. Lipids also include fatty acids and their derivatives, such as triglycerides, diglycerides, monoglycerides, and phospholipids, as well as sterol-containing molecules like cholesterol. Lipids can be classified into eight major categories based on their biochemical building blocks, which are derived from ketoacyl and isoprene groups. These categories include fatty acyls, glycerolipids, glycerophospholipids, sphingolipids, sterol lipids, prenol lipids, saccharolipids, and polyketides. Fatty Acyls Fatty acyls, including fatty acids, are synthesized through the elongation of an acetyl-CoA primer with malonyl-CoA or methylmalonyl-CoA. These molecules are fundamental building blocks of complex lipids. Fatty acyls can be saturated or unsaturated and may contain functional groups with oxygen, halogens, nitrogen, or sulfur. Biologically significant fatty acyls include eicosanoids, which are derived from arachidonic acid and include prostaglandins, leukotrienes, and thromboxanes. Other subclasses include fatty esters (e.g., wax esters, fatty acyl thioesters, and fatty acyl carnitines) and fatty amides (e.g., N-acyl ethanolamines like anandamide). Glycerolipids Glycerolipids are primarily composed of mono-, di-, and tri-substituted glycerols. The most well-known glycerolipids are triacylglycerols (triglycerides), which serve as the main storage form of fat in animal tissues. Other subclasses include glycosylglycerols, which have sugar residues attached to glycerol. Examples include digalactosyldiacylglycerols in plant membranes and seminolipids in mammalian sperm. Glycerophospholipids Glycerophospholipids, also known as phospholipids, are essential components of cell membranes and play roles in metabolism and signaling. They consist of a glycerol backbone linked to two fatty acid chains and a polar head group via a phosphate ester bond. Examples include phosphatidylcholine (lecithin), phosphatidylethanolamine, and phosphatidylserine. Some glycerophospholipids, such as phosphatidylinositols and phosphatidic acids, act as precursors or second messengers in signaling pathways. Sphingolipids Sphingolipids are a complex family of lipids that share a sphingoid base backbone, synthesized from serine and long-chain fatty acyl-CoA. They are further converted into ceramides, phosphosphingolipids, and glycosphingolipids. Ceramides, which are N-acyl-sphingoid bases, are a major subclass. Sphingomyelins are the primary phosphosphingolipids in mammals, while glycosphingolipids include cerebrosides and gangliosides, which are involved in cell recognition and signaling. Sterol Lipids Sterol lipids, such as cholesterol, are integral components of cell membranes and precursors to steroid hormones. Steroids, which share a four-ring core structure, include estrogens, androgens (e.g., testosterone), progestogens, glucocorticoids, and mineralocorticoids. Secosteroids, such as vitamin D, are characterized by a broken B-ring. Bile acids, derived from cholesterol, aid in digestion and are synthesized in the liver. Prenol Lipids Prenol lipids are synthesized from isopentenyl diphosphate and dimethylallyl diphosphate via the mevalonic acid pathway. They include simple isoprenoids, carotenoids (antioxidants and vitamin A precursors), and quinones like ubiquinones (coenzyme Q). Polyprenols, such as dolichols, play roles in glycosylation and membrane transport. Saccharolipids Saccharolipids are lipids in which fatty acids are directly linked to a sugar backbone. They are compatible with membrane bilayers and include lipid A, a component of lipopolysaccharides in Gram-negative bacteria. Lipid A molecules are disaccharides of glucosamine with multiple fatty-acyl chains. Polyketides Polyketides are synthesized by polymerization of acetyl and propionyl subunits. They are structurally diverse and include many secondary metabolites with antimicrobial, antiparasitic, and anticancer properties, such as erythromycin and tetracycline. Biological Functions of Lipids Membranes Glycerophospholipids are the primary structural components of biological membranes, forming lipid bilayers that separate intracellular and extracellular environments. These amphipathic molecules have hydrophilic heads and hydrophobic tails, which self-assemble in aqueous environments to form bilayers or micelles. Other lipids, such as sphingomyelin and cholesterol, also contribute to membrane structure and function. In plants and algae, galactosyldiacylglycerols and sulfoquinovosyldiacylglycerols are key membrane components in chloroplasts. Energy Storage and Metabolism Triacylglycerols stored in adipose tissue are the primary energy reserves in animals, providing 9 kcal/g. Fatty acids are broken down via beta-oxidation in mitochondria or peroxisomes to generate acetyl-CoA, which enters the citric acid cycle to produce ATP. Fatty acid synthesis occurs in the cytoplasm, using acetyl-CoA as a precursor. Lipids are also packaged into lipoproteins for transport. Signaling Lipids play critical roles in cell signaling. Examples include sphingosine-1-phosphate, which regulates calcium mobilization and apoptosis; diacylglycerol (DAG) and phosphatidylinositol phosphates (PIPs), which activate protein kinase C; prostaglandins, which mediate inflammation; and steroid hormones like estrogen and testosterone, which regulate reproduction and metabolism. Other Functions Fat-soluble vitamins (A, D, E, and K) are essential nutrients with diverse roles, including vision, bone health, and antioxidant activity. Acyl-carnitines facilitate fatty acid transport into mitochondria, while polyprenols are involved in glycosylation and polysaccharide biosynthesis. Cardiolipins, found in mitochondrial membranes, are crucial for oxidative phosphorylation. Nutrition and Health Lipids are essential for life but can also contribute to disease. Essential fatty acids, such as linoleic acid (omega-6) and alpha-linolenic acid (omega-3), must be obtained from the diet. These fatty acids influence cell membrane composition and function. High-fat diets, particularly those rich in saturated fats and trans fats, are associated with obesity, diabetes, and atherosclerosis. Atherosclerosis, characterized by cholesterol-rich plaques in arteries, is a leading cause of cardiovascular disease. Dietary modifications, such as increasing monounsaturated fats (e.g., olive oil) and reducing saturated fats, can improve lipid profiles and reduce cardiovascular risk. Statins, which inhibit cholesterol synthesis, are commonly used to manage hypercholesterolemia.
